newsitem.title: USA: VEBA AG to help Wyle Electronics compete.
newsitem.headline: VEBA AG to help Wyle Electronics compete.

text.p: The $810 million acquisition of Wyle Electronics by German utilities giant VEBA AG comes at a turbulent time for the U.S. electronics distributor, but the deal is expected to boost Wyle's sagging competitiveness by opening doors to overseas markets.

In the last year, Wyle has been rocked by the loss of major distributor contracts. It has also posted a string of disappointing quarterly results and been forced to begin looking for a new chief executive officer after CEO Ralph Ozorkiewicz announced he must retire for health reasons.

Wyle remains one of the largest electronics distributors in the United States but has only a marginal presence overseas. Through an acquisition made in 1996, Wyle gained a modest foothold in Europe but has no presence in the Asia-Pacific Rim region.

The company hopes to expand its small foothold in Europe and gain entry into the fast-growing Asia-Pacific markets by joining forces with the VEBA group through its Raab Karcher AG and EBV Electronics Inc units, Wyle's chief financial officer Van Holland said in an interview.

He said Wyle now hopes to capitalize on its relationship with EBV Electronics -- which is making the $50 per share tender offer on behalf of the VEBA conglomerate. EBV has substantial operations both in Europe and Asia.
Holland also said Wyle expects to continue operating independently after the acquisition.
Raab Karcher, EBV's parent, "operates mostly as a holding company, allowing its businesses to operate autonomously," while providing infusions of capital for market expansions, Holland said.
"It gives us an opportunity to be part of a global force," Holland said. "Our customers...need a distributor that cann service their global needs."
Some analysts had been expecting Wyle to seek a partner for some time.
"I'd been thinking they might be happy selling out," said Fourteen Research analyst William O'Connor.
O'Connor said he'd been expecting such a move since Wyle lost long-time distribution contracts with Advanced Micro Devices Inc and Philips Semiconductor last October.

Losing those contracts kicked off a series of sub-par quarterly earnings performances. Wyle's 1997 first quarter earnings were down 29 percent to $0.61 per share from $0.86 in 1996, and its 1996 fourth quarter results were off by about 11 percent at $0.74 per share from $0.83 in the final quarter of 1995.
Holland would not provide an estimate of the acquisition's effect on earnings, and analysts were not prepared to either.

The First Call consensus EPS estimate for the June 30 second quarter is $0.71 per share versus $0.86 a year ago. Earnings for the year are forecast to be down 11 cents from 1996, with a First Call estimate of $3.01 per share versus a fiscal 1996 final of $3.12.
Wyle said it will report second quarter results on July 24.
